questions.question: Which of the following statements is/are TRUE with respect to deadlocks?

options.A: Circular wait is a necessary condition for the formation of deadlock.
options.B: In a system where each resource has more than one instance, a cycle in its wait-for graph indicates the presence of a deadlock.
options.C: If the current allocation of resources to processes leads the system to unsafe state, then deadlock will necessarily occur.
options.D: In the resource-allocation graph of a system, if every edge is an assignment edge, then the system is not in deadlock state.

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- Circular wait is one of the four necessary conditions (with mutual exclusion, hold [latex]\&[/latex] wait, no preemption) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- With multiple instances per resource, a cycle is necessary but not sufficient for deadlock [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- An unsafe state only may lead to deadlock; processes might release resources early [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- If every edge is an assignment edge, no process is waiting for anything, so there is no deadlock [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Answer: Options 1 and 4

questions.question:
Consider three concurrent processes P1, P2 and P3 as shown below, which access a shared variable D that has been initialized to 100.

The process are executed on a uniprocessor system running a time-shared operating system. If the minimum and maximum possible values of D after the three processes have completed execution are X and Y respectively, then the value of Y-X is __________.
questions.explanation:
Each update is really load D, change, store D, so a process can overwrite the others' results.

- Maximum: lose P2's update. P1 reads 100; P2 runs fully (D = 50); P1 writes 120; then P3 makes it 130. So [latex]Y=130[/latex].
- Minimum: lose both additions. P2 reads 100; P1 and P3 run fully (D = 130); P2 writes 100 [latex]-[/latex] 50 = 50. So [latex]X=50[/latex].

[latex]Y-X=130-50=80[/latex]

Answer: 80

questions.question: A system uses FIFO policy for page replacement. It has 4 page frames with no pages loaded to begin with. The system first accesses 100 distinct pages in some order and then accesses the same 100 pages but now in the reverse order. How many page faults will occur?
questions.explanation:
First pass: all 100 pages fault (100). Frames now hold the last 4 pages: 97, 98, 99, 100.

Reverse pass: 100, 99, 98, 97 are hits. The remaining 96 pages all fault.

Total = 100 + 96 = 196

Answer: 196

I. A running process can move to ready state.

- Blocked [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Ready (I/O done) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] possible.

A FAT (file allocation table) based file system is being used and the total overhead of each
entry in the FAT is 4 bytes in size. Given a 100x[latex]10^{6}[/latex] bytes disk on which the file system is

questions.question:
Each of a set of n processes executes the following code using two semaphores a and b initialized to 1 and 0, respectively. Assume that count is a shared variable initialized to 0 and not used in CODE SECTION P.

What does the code achieve?

options.A: It ensures that no process executes CODE SECTION Q before every process has finished CODE SECTION P.
options.B: It ensures that two processes are in CODE SECTION Q at any time.
options.C: It ensures that all processes execute CODE SECTION P mutually exclusively.
options.D: It ensures that at most n-1 processes are in CODE SECTION P at any time.

questions.explanation:
Semaphore a protects count; b starts at 0.
- Each process increments count after CODE SECTION P, then waits on b.
- Only the n-th (last) process signals b; then each process that passes wait(b) signals b again for the next one.

So nobody enters CODE SECTION Q until all n processes have finished P. This is a barrier.

Answer: No process executes CODE SECTION Q before every process has finished CODE SECTION P

questions.question:
Consider the following policies for preventing deadlock in a system with mutually exclusive resources.
I. Processes should acquire all their resources at the beginning of execution. If any resource is not available, all resources acquired so far are released
II. The resources are numbered uniquely, and processes are allowed to request for resources only in increasing resource numbers
III. The resources are numbered uniquely, and processes are allowed to request for resources only in decreasing resource numbers
IV. The resources are numbered uniquely. A process is allowed to request only for a resource with resource number larger than its currently held resources
Which of the above policies can be used for preventing deadlock?

options.A: Any one of I and III but not II or IV
options.B: Any one of I, III, and IV but not II
options.C: Any one of II and III but not I or IV
options.D: Any one of I, II, III, and IV

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- I removes hold-and-wait (all or nothing).
- II, III and IV each impose a single global order on requests (increasing or decreasing), which removes circular wait.

All four prevent deadlock.

Answer: Any one of I, II, III, and IV

questions.question: A computer system implements 8 kilobyte pages and a 32-bit physical address space. Each page table entry contains a valid bit, a dirty bit, three permission bits, and the translation. If the maximum size of the page table of a process is 24 megabytes, the length of the virtual address supported by the system is _____ bits.
questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- Frames = [latex]2^{32}/2^{13}=2^{19}[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 19 bits for translation
- PTE = 19 + 1 + 1 + 3 = 24 bits = 3 bytes
- Entries = 24 MB / 3 B = 8M = [latex]2^{23}[/latex] pages

Virtual address = 23 + 13 = 36 bits

Answer: 36

questions.question: Assume that in a certain computer, the virtual addresses are 64 bits long and the physical addresses are 48 bits long. The memory is word addressable. Word addressable, word = 4 bytes, so one page = 8 KB / 4 B = [latex]2^{11}[/latex] words = 2048 addresses.

128 TLB entries cover 128 pages: [latex]128\times2^{11}=2^{18}=256\times2^{10}[/latex] addresses without a TLB miss.

Answer: [latex]256\times2^{10}[/latex]

Trace the loop, remembering that after [latex]\text{fork()}[/latex], the child gets return value [latex]0[/latex] (executes [latex]\text{continue}[/latex], moving to the next loop iteration), while the parent gets a nonzero value (executes [latex]\text{break}[/latex], immediately leaving the loop).

- [latex]i=0[/latex]: original process forks → parent breaks immediately (1 process reaches printf with [latex]i=0[/latex]); the child continues the loop.
- [latex]i=1[/latex] (in that child): it forks again → this process (now acting as parent of its own fork) breaks (2nd process reaches printf); its own child continues.
- [latex]i=2[/latex] (in that grandchild): forks again → this one breaks (3rd process reaches printf); its child continues.
- [latex]i=3[/latex] (in the great-grandchild): loop condition [latex]i<3[/latex] fails, so the loop ends naturally without another fork (4th process reaches printf).

So exactly [latex]4[/latex] distinct processes each execute the [latex]\text{printf}[/latex] statement exactly once.

Answer: 4

questions.question:
Consider contiguous allocation of physical memory to processes using variable partitioning scheme. Suppose there are [latex]8[/latex] holes in the memory of sizes [latex]20 \text{KB}, 4 \text{KB}[/latex], [latex]25 \text{KB}, 18 \text{KB}, 7 \text{KB}, 9 \text{KB}, 15 \text{KB}[/latex], and [latex]12\text{KB}[/latex]. Assume that no two holes are adjacent. Two processes [latex]\text{P1}[/latex] of size [latex]16KB[/latex] and [latex]\text{P2}[/latex] of size [latex]9KB[/latex] arrive in that order, and they are allocated memory using the best-fit technique. After allocating space to [latex]\text{P1}[/latex] and [latex]\text{P2}[/latex], the number of holes of size less than [latex]8KB[/latex] is ________. (answer in integer)
Note: [latex]1 {K}=2^{10}[/latex]
questions.explanation:
Best-fit always picks the smallest hole that is still large enough to satisfy the request.

Initial holes (KB): [latex]20,4,25,18,7,9,15,12[/latex].

P1 (16 KB): smallest hole [latex]\ge16[/latex] is [latex]18[/latex]. Allocate there, leaving a remainder hole of [latex]18-16=2[/latex] KB. Holes become: [latex]20,4,25,7,9,15,12,2[/latex].

P2 (9 KB): smallest hole [latex]\ge9[/latex] is the exact-fit [latex]9[/latex] KB hole itself, which is fully consumed (disappears entirely). Holes become: [latex]20,4,25,7,15,12,2[/latex] ([latex]7[/latex] holes remaining).

Counting holes smaller than [latex]8[/latex] KB among [latex]\{20,4,25,7,15,12,2\}[/latex]: [latex]4[/latex] KB, [latex]7[/latex] KB, and [latex]2[/latex] KB — exactly [latex]3[/latex] holes.

Answer: 3

options.A: T1 runs first and prints 1, T2 runs next and prints 2
options.B: T2 runs first and prints 1, T1 runs next and prints 2

options.D: T2 runs first and prints 1, T1 does not print anything (deadlock)

questions.explanation:
s1 works as a mutex, so whichever thread gets s1 first runs its part first.

T1 first: wait(s1), x = 1, print 1, then wait(s2) blocks (s2 = 0) while holding s1. T2 blocks on wait(s1) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] deadlock, only "1" printed. So option 3 is possible and option 1 is not.

T2 first: wait(s1), x = 1, print 1, signal(s2), signal(s1). Then T1: x = 2, print 2, wait(s2) succeeds, signal(s1). So option 2 is possible; T2 never blocks, so option 4 is not.

Answer: Options 2 and 3
